questions.q: A coach says 'Watch the next bird.' What will you see?

options.text: A live pigeon released from a box
A clay target thrown by a trap
A bird-shaped paper target on a board

questions.explain: 'Bird' is shooters' slang for a clay target; the FITASC rules forbid shooting at live animals.

questions.q: What does a shotgun fire?
questions.explain: The shot leaves the muzzle as a small cloud of pellets, so the shooter points ahead of the moving target.

questions.q: Which statement about Compak® Sporting is correct?

options.text: A compact version on one field, stations in a line
It is the Olympic version of the Skeet discipline
It is shot only at live game birds in the field
It uses a single trap and a single station

questions.explain: Compak® Sporting brings Sporting™-style targets onto one small field with five stations and six traps.

questions.q: What do you shoot at in clay shooting?

options.text: Live birds released from a box
Clay targets thrown by a trap
Paper targets fixed on a board

questions.explain: You shoot only at artificial targets thrown by a trap. Shooting at live animals is forbidden.

questions.q: What is a trap?

options.text: A shotgun with a short barrel
The referee who runs the stand

questions.explain: A trap is the machine that throws a target into the air or rolls it along the ground.

questions.q: Why does a shooter point the gun ahead of a moving target?

options.text: The shot needs time to reach the target
The referee asks all shooters to do it
It keeps the gun from touching the target

questions.explain: The target moves and the shot takes time to get there, so the gun points where the target will be a moment later.

questions.q: How many targets does one Sporting™ layout give?
questions.explain: Each layout gives 25 targets: 15 singles and 5 doubles (a double is two targets, so 10 more).

questions.q: How many traps are there on one Compak field?

options.text: Two, a high and a low one

questions.explain: A Compak® Sporting field has 6 traps lettered A to F and 5 shooting stations in a line.

questions.q: In which discipline do targets come from two houses, a high one and a low one?
questions.explain: Skeet has a high house and a low house, with the stations on a half-circle between them.

questions.q: Your first shot misses a single target. What does the rule allow?

options.text: You must open the gun at once
You may fire the second barrel

questions.explain: In Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting a single target must allow two shots, so a miss with the first can still be followed by the second.

questions.q: Does a spectator need hearing protection?

options.text: No, only the people who are shooting
Yes, the rules require it near the layout
Only at championships, not at club shoots

questions.explain: Both rulebooks require hearing protection for shooters, referees, staff and spectators near the layout.

questions.q: May you take photos with flash?

options.text: Yes, if you stay in the spectator area
Only once the referee has agreed
No, because flash can dazzle the shooter

questions.explain: Flash distracts and dazzles the shooter, so spectators do not use it.

questions.q: What happens if a spectator coaches a shooter during a competition?

options.text: The shooter can get a yellow card; the adviser is sent away
Nothing at all, as long as the advice is given quietly
The shooter must shoot the whole stand again from the start

questions.explain: Advice during a competition counts as coaching, which both rulebooks forbid.

questions.q: When is it right to applaud?

options.text: While the shooter is aiming at the target
After the stand, when nobody is about to call

questions.explain: While anyone on the layout is shooting or about to call, spectators stay quiet; applause comes when the shooter has finished.

questions.q: Where may a spectator stand?

options.text: In front of the firing line, for a better view
Next to the traps, out of the line of fire
In the spectator area, behind the stand

questions.explain: Spectators stand in the area set aside for them, usually behind the stand.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting, a spectator loudly criticises a ruling. How do the rules see this?

options.text: As an attempt to influence the referee
As normal support from the crowd
As a breach of the dress code

questions.explain: In Compak® Sporting the rules count open criticism of a decision by shooters or spectators, without the referee’s permission, as an attempt to influence.

questions.q: What do you need to film a competition with a drone?

options.text: Nothing, as long as it flies above the stands
The organiser’s permission, plus the country’s drone rules
Permission from one of the shooters in the squad

questions.explain: Flying over a shooting ground needs the organiser’s permission, and the drone rules of the country always apply.

questions.q: Which target rolls and bounces along the ground?
questions.explain: A rabbit is a thick, strong target rolled on its edge along the ground.

questions.q: Which kind of double exists only in Sporting™?
questions.explain: A Compak® Sporting double is on report or simultaneous; the rafale belongs to Sporting™ only.

questions.q: What should stay the same in a good pre-shot routine?
questions.explain: Many coaches suggest the same steps in the same order; the time may vary a little within the time limit.

questions.q: What is a double on report?

options.text: The shot at the first target releases the second
Both targets are released at the same moment
One target is shot at twice

questions.explain: The sound of the first shot releases the second target.

questions.q: Where is the stock of a Sporting™ shooter before the target appears?

options.text: Below the line on the vest

questions.explain: In Sporting™ the top of the stock stays below the line on the vest until the target appears; in Compak® Sporting the gun position at the call is free.

questions.q: Which presentation usually needs the most lead?

options.text: An incomer flying straight at the shooter
A crosser at the same distance

questions.explain: All of a crosser's speed is sideways, so you shoot furthest in front of it; targets flying straight away from you or towards you need little sideways lead.

questions.q: A target comes towards the shooter at an angle and passes to the side. What is it called?
questions.explain: Quartering towards (or quartering in) is an angled target coming in; quartering away is the angled target moving off.

questions.q: Why should a target be read from the exact stand you will shoot from?

options.text: One trap can give a different angle from each stand
The rules forbid watching from any other place
Targets change colour from one stand to the next
Only the referee may stand anywhere else

questions.explain: The angle between the shooter and the target's line changes with the position, so the presentation changes too.

questions.q: A crosser flies far from you. Compared with a near one at the same speed, it needs…
questions.explain: The further the target, the further it travels while the shot is on its way, so it needs more lead.

questions.q: A crosser is slowing down at your break point. Compared with one at full speed, it needs…
questions.explain: A slower target moves less while the shot travels, so it needs less lead.

questions.q: From whose point of view are “left” and “right” given for a crosser?
questions.explain: Directions are the shooter's: an L→R crosser flies from the shooter's left to right.

questions.q: The coach says “long crosser”. What does “long” mean?

options.text: The target flies for a long time
The target is a long, oval clay
The shooter should wait a long time

questions.explain: In coaching “long” describes distance. A long crosser is a far crosser, which needs more lead.

questions.q: What is true of crossers in Compak® Sporting?

options.text: Crossers are not allowed on a Compak
Crossers may only be thrown as rabbits
An L→R and an R→L crosser are compulsory

questions.explain: The Compak® Sporting rules make three trajectories compulsory: an L→R crosser, an R→L crosser and a going-away target.

questions.q: How does the lead on a quartering target compare with a full crosser at the same distance and speed?

options.text: It is the same as the crosser
It is larger than the crosser
It is smaller, depending on the angle

questions.explain: Only the sideways part of the movement needs sideways lead, so the closer the target is to a straight line away from you or towards you, the smaller the lead.

questions.q: In a report pair, what releases the second target?

options.text: The shot at the first target

questions.explain: “On report” means on the sound of the shot: firing at the first target releases the second.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting a shooter deliberately fires both cartridges at the first target of a simultaneous double. Result?

options.text: Only the second target is zero

questions.explain: Compak® Sporting allows one cartridge per target of a double; deliberately firing both at one target is scored zero-zero. In Sporting™ it would be allowed.

questions.q: In which discipline are there rafale doubles?
questions.explain: A rafale is two targets from one trap on one trajectory, a Sporting™ double. Compak® Sporting has only doubles on report and simultaneous doubles.

questions.q: A British coach says “true pair”. How do you translate it?
questions.explain: “True pair” is the English Sporting name for a simultaneous pair; “true” has nothing to do with correctness.

questions.q: How many targets does one Sporting™ layout give?
questions.explain: Each Sporting™ layout type gives 25 targets: 15 singles and 5 doubles.

questions.q: In Sporting™ one shot breaks both targets of a double. How is it scored?

options.text: No Bird, the double is repeated

questions.explain: In Sporting™ both targets count when one shot breaks them. Compak® Sporting has different rules.

questions.q: On a FITASC score card, what does O mean?
questions.explain: On the standard FITASC card a hit is marked X and a miss O.

questions.q: In Compak® Sporting your shooter refuses to sign the score sheet. What is the consequence?

options.text: He loses the right to make any complaint
The referee signs and nothing changes

questions.explain: The Compak® Sporting rules say a shooter who refuses to sign loses the right to complain.

questions.q: You want to compare the scores of two shooters. What is a fair way to do it?

options.text: Compare the percentages, whatever the length of the event
Compare only the highest round each of them shot
Compare them over the same number of targets, preferably at one event

questions.explain: The same percentage over a different number of targets, or at other grounds, is not the same test: layouts differ in difficulty.

questions.q: How are ties for the top three places settled?
questions.explain: For the top three there is a 25-target shoot-off, then sudden death.

questions.q: In Sporting™, when must you check your score on the card?

options.text: Only at the end of the day

questions.explain: Check your score when leaving each stand and raise any disagreement at once; later there is no appeal.

questions.q: In Sporting™, what does the referee do with the score card before the squad moves to the next stand?

options.text: Takes it to the jury straight away
Pins it on the central scoreboard

questions.explain: Before the squad moves on, the referee photographs the card and marks with an asterisk the shooter who carries it to the next stand.

questions.q: How does a category differ from a class?

options.text: They mean the same thing in the rules
A category is by results, a class by age
A category is by age or sex, a class by results

questions.explain: Junior, Lady, Senior and Veteran are categories by age or sex; AA, A, B and C are national classes by average score.

questions.q: How are tied shooters below third place ranked?

options.text: They share it; countback from the 8th layout sets the order
By a shoot-off of 25 targets for the place
By drawing lots after the event has ended

questions.explain: There are no shoot-offs below third place: the place is shared and countback sets the order, from the 8th layout or Compak back to the 1st.

questions.q: A shooter born in 1971 enters a FITASC competition in 2027. Which category?
questions.explain: He turns 56 in 2027, so he is Senior from 1 January, whatever his birthday.

questions.q: How many targets are in the first round of a shoot-off?
questions.explain: A shoot-off is a round of 25 targets; if the scores are still level, sudden death follows.

questions.q: Two shooters tie for 7th place. What happens?

options.text: A coin toss by the jury
They share the place and are ordered by countback

questions.explain: Shoot-offs are only for places 1–3; below that, tied shooters are listed by countback from the eighth layout or Compak.

questions.q: From what age can women and girls enter the Lady category under FITASC rules?

options.text: From 1 January of the year they turn 13
From the day of their 18th birthday
From 1 January of the year they turn 21

questions.explain: Lady starts from the year of the 13th birthday, counted by year of birth.

questions.q: Does the Lady category have an upper age limit?

options.text: Yes, it ends at the age of 55
No, the FITASC table sets none
Yes, it ends at the age of 40

questions.explain: The FITASC table sets no upper limit for Lady.

questions.q: Do women shoot shorter or easier trajectories?

options.text: No, the targets are the same for all

questions.explain: The category affects only the ranking, not the targets.

questions.q: How should you translate the FITASC category “Senior” for a client?
questions.explain: In FITASC Senior is an age group of 56–65; the main adult category is Men.

questions.q: How many shooters are in a Men team in Sporting™?
questions.explain: Teams usually have three shooters, but the Men team in Sporting™ has four.

questions.q: What are shooter profiles on ClayArena built from?
questions.explain: A profile gathers the shooter's competitions, that is, competition results.

questions.q: What is ClayAway today?
questions.explain: ClayAway will be ClayArena's organised training tours with a coach; it has not launched yet.

questions.q: Where do you look for competitions that have not happened yet?
questions.explain: The calendar lists planned, ongoing and finished competitions with dates and venues.

questions.q: Which disciplines is ClayArena focused on?
questions.explain: ClayArena is focused on these two FITASC disciplines; some other disciplines appear there too.

questions.q: Where do the results on ClayArena come from?
questions.explain: Results come from the score sheets, so check your score while you are still at the ground.

questions.q: How many targets does an international Sporting™ competition usually have?
questions.explain: The FITASC rules set 200 targets in rounds of 25 for international events.

questions.q: You cannot find your name. What can you try?
questions.explain: Names are written as in the competition documents: in Latin letters or in the local alphabet. The same surname can also be written in Latin letters in more than one way.

questions.q: When does a Compak® Sporting shooter sign the score sheet?

options.text: At the end of each round
The referee signs, not the shooter

questions.explain: The shooter signs at the end of each round; without a signature no later complaint is accepted.

questions.q: In Sporting™, when should you check your score on the card?

options.text: At the end of the season

questions.explain: Check it when you leave each stand and tell the referee at once if something is wrong.

questions.q: A shooter broke 150 targets out of 200. What is the accuracy?
What is the performance index in a ClayArena profile?

options.text: One number worked out by ClayArena
The number of events in a year

questions.explain: It is a ClayArena figure for following progress, not an official ranking.

questions.q: Why do the figures from one competition say little?

options.text: Nobody can reach the top 10 there
Layouts and weather differ a lot

questions.explain: That is why figures over several competitions are more reliable.

questions.q: What is a perfect round?

options.text: A round shot within one hour

questions.explain: A perfect round has no miss. In the FITASC disciplines that is a round with all 25 targets broken.

questions.q: You shot 90 out of 100 at a club shoot and 180 out of 200 at an international event. What can you compare?
questions.explain: With different numbers of targets, compare the accuracy rather than the totals. Layouts, weather and the level of the event still differ, so treat it as a rough guide.

questions.q: How can you learn more from a competition video?

options.text: Follow one shooter and one detail
Listen only to the sound of the shots
Look only at the final scores

questions.explain: Watching piece by piece, one shooter at a time, teaches you the most.

questions.q: What does the ClayArena competition calendar show?
questions.explain: The calendar helps you find a competition to go to or to follow.

questions.q: What is the break point?
questions.explain: The break point is where the shooter plans to break the target.

questions.q: What can a beginner learn from competition videos?

options.text: Who will win the next event

questions.explain: Videos are a visual lesson in technique and rules.

questions.q: Where do you check a competition's entry conditions and schedule?
questions.explain: The organiser sets the entry conditions and the schedule.

questions.q: What do season recaps show?
questions.explain: Season recaps are a short overview of the year in the sport.

questions.q: How long does a Compak® Sporting shooter have to call for the target after the shooter on the previous station has fired?
questions.explain: A Compak® Sporting shooter has at most 10 seconds to call, counted from the shot at the previous station's target. The 15-second limit is a Sporting™ rule.

questions.q: Who decides whether a target was hit?

options.text: The squad, by a show of hands
The referee, and the referee alone
The shooter, by checking the pieces

questions.explain: Only the referee decides; the squad does not step in unless the referee asks.

questions.q: How do you properly disagree with a referee’s decision?

options.text: At once on the stand: raise your hand and say “protest”
After the round, with a post on social media
By arguing until the referee changes his mind

questions.explain: A protest is made at once, on the stand; arguing afterwards counts as an attempt to influence.

questions.q: A squad-mate loudly tells the referee he is wrong about a hit. How do the rules see this?

options.text: As useful information for the referee
As a formal protest by the squad
As an attempt to influence the referee
As normal chat with no consequence

questions.explain: Others openly criticising a ruling without the referee’s permission count as an attempt to influence; only the shooter concerned may protest.

questions.q: What can happen after aggressive behaviour towards the referee?

options.text: Nothing, if the shooter apologises later
The jury may expel the shooter
The shooter shoots the next target again

questions.explain: The referee reports it to the jury, which may expel the shooter from the competition.
